highlights: The 89th Imperial Diet dissolved after passing the Trade Union Law, the Agricultural Lands Adjustment Law, and an Election Law establishing women's suffrage.
SCAP issued the Shinto Directive on 15 December, completely separating State Shinto from governmental administration, public finance, and school curricula.
Militaristic and ultra-nationalistic textbooks in morals, geography, and Japanese history were banned by SCAP directive on 21 December pending replacement.
Former Prime Minister Prince Fumimaro Konoye committed suicide on 16 December rather than surrender as an indicted major war criminal suspect.
In Japan's first war crimes trial at Yokohama, military commission judges convicted Tatsuo Tsuchiya of prisoner abuse and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
Eighteen major holding companies, including Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda, and Sumitomo, and 325 subsidiaries were designated as restricted concerns for dissolution.
Announcement of the Moscow Conference's four-power trusteeship plan provoked massive nationwide Korean protests, strikes, and demonstrations coordinated by Kim Koo's Anti-Trusteeship Committee.
Lieutenant General John R. Hodge publicly denounced the Korean People's Republic, declaring Military Government the sole lawful governing authority in South Korea.

sections.summary: General Orders No. 20 established the International Prosecution Section for war crimes trials, while Civil Administration in Korea created the Provincial Affairs and Korean Civil Service Sections.
sections.title: Organization Under SCAP

sections.summary: The 89th Diet passed election, agrarian land, and trade union laws before dissolving; Prince Konoye committed suicide to avoid war crime arrest; and Tatsuo Tsuchiya received a life sentence in the first Yokohama war crimes trial.
sections.title: Political Activities in Japan

sections.summary: Coal production rose 53 percent to 840,000 metric tons; the first Trade Union Law was enacted; eighteen holding companies and 325 subsidiaries were designated restricted concerns; and Bank of Japan note issues expanded.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Japan

sections.summary: State Shinto was separated from government support; militaristic textbooks in morals, geography, and history were banned; census figures showed sharp population declines in major cities; and over 654,000 repatriates departed Japan.
sections.title: Social Activities in Japan

sections.summary: The Moscow Conference's announcement of a four-power trusteeship provoked nationwide Korean resentment; political coalition efforts continued under Kim Koo; and free marketing of rice was ordered suspended as of 1 January 1946.
sections.title: Civil Administration in Korea

sections.summary: Surveys political developments, public safety, legal affairs, and war crimes prosecutions in Japan.
sections.title: Part II: Political - Japan

sections.summary: The 89th Diet passed women's suffrage, land reform, and trade union laws before dissolution; numerous parties formed, including the Japan Cooperative and New Japan Women's parties; and the Cabinet abolished the Board of Information.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Metropolitan Tokyo crime statistics showed no postwar crime wave; the Economic Police Section was eliminated during police demilitarization; political prisoners had their voting rights restored; and hidden military aircraft engines were seized in Shizuoka.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Seven directives ordered the arrest of 205 war criminal suspects, bringing Sugamo Prison internments to 445; Tatsuo Tsuchiya received a life sentence at Yokohama; and trials of camp commanders Yuri and Furushima commenced.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Surveys Japanese natural resources, manufacturing, commerce, finance, and industrial labor conditions.
sections.title: Part III: Economic - Japan

sections.summary: Government rice collection lagged at 30 percent of quota, prompting increased purchase prices and subsidies; soil surveys evaluated reclamation potential; and naval fuel oil releases stimulated commercial fish landings while curbing black-market sales.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Surveys detailed operations at Japan's largest modern sawmill and the Amagi Imperial Forest; coal production rebounded 53 percent to 840,000 tons; and declassified wartime data revealed excessive overexpansion in subsidized mining industries.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Steel operations remained depressed at five percent of capacity; 228 vessels underwent repair in shipyards; the textile industry reorganized into a democratic association; and the Diet repealed sixteen major wartime industrial control laws.
sections.title: Industry

sections.summary: Coastal tankers transported vital petroleum products; seventeen radio navigation beacons were restored; domestic electric heater use caused urban distribution system overloads; and coal shortages restricted gas service in Tokyo to three hours daily.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: Imperial Ordinance established the Board of Trade to manage foreign commerce; imports were limited to salt and kerosene, while coal and silkworm eggs were exported; and an inventory was ordered for 50,000 exportable silk bales.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Promulgation of the Labor Union Law catalyzed rapid unionization across mining and transport; workers settled major disputes at Yomiuri and Keisei Railway with wage increases; and occupational registration recorded 3.19 million unemployed persons.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: Trunk cable reconstruction advanced, Sender Composition Message service to the United States handled record holiday traffic, 1946 radio receiver production was projected at 3.1 million sets, and captured military communications equipment was disassembled for civilian parts.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: Critical urban food reserves dipped to two-to-eight days; government rice purchase prices and producer subsidies were increased; official fish ceiling prices were reestablished; and petroleum prices surged 280 to 400 percent following subsidy abolition.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note circulation expanded to 51.09 billion yen driven by government advances and commercial borrowing; monthly bank condition reporting was instituted; and repatriates were permitted to bring in yen-denominated savings books and bonds.
sections.title: Money and Banking

sections.summary: Diet supplementary budgets funded food and salt production; military pensions were suspended, reducing war expenses; the Big Four Zaibatsu reported 3.15 billion yen in assets; and SCAP placed eighteen holding companies under strict financial restrictions.
sections.title: Public Finance

sections.summary: Reports on public health, medical administration, welfare, education, religious directives, and media democratization in Japan.
sections.title: Part IV: Social - Japan

sections.summary: DDT dusting checked typhus outbreaks among Hokkaido coal miners; military hospitals were transferred to civilian use, doubling bed capacity; the November census recorded 71,996,477 residents; and a 30,000-person nutrition survey was conducted in Tokyo.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: SCAP issued the historic Shinto Directive abolishing state sponsorship and banned militaristic textbooks in morals, geography, and history; an American educational mission was requested; and media programs broadcast the 'Now It Can Be Told' war history.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: Covers political, economic, and social activities under US military government in South Korea.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: Announcement of a four-power trusteeship at the Moscow Conference ignited widespread Korean strikes and anti-trusteeship mass demonstrations led by Kim Koo; General Hodge repudiated the Korean People's Republic; and a National Bar Association was established.
sections.title: Political Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Despite a 15.97-million-koku rice harvest, market withholding forced the suspension of free trading and reinstatement of price ceilings; Japanese-owned agricultural lands were transferred to the New Korea Company; and Japanese branch banks were merged into Korean institutions.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Korea

sections.summary: A Korean was appointed Director of Education; Korean Pacific Press began independent operations with Associated Press; Seoul University graduated its first public health class; and emergency diphtheria antitoxin shipments were flown in from Japan.
sections.title: Social Activities in Korea

summary: Monthly Summation No. 3 covers non-military activities of GHQ/SCAP in Japan and USAMGIK in southern Korea during December 1945. In Japan, decisive structural reforms reshaped political and social life. The extraordinary Diet session enacted landmark democratic legislation, including the Trade Union Law, the Agricultural Lands Adjustment Law, and an Election Law granting women suffrage. Concurrently, SCAP directives disestablished State Shinto, banned militaristic textbooks, ordered dissolution of eighteen Zaibatsu holding companies, and established the International Prosecution Section. War crimes proceedings intensified with the apprehension of 205 high-ranking suspects—precipitating Prince Fumimaro Konoye's suicide—and the first Yokohama military trial convicting Tatsuo Tsuchiya. Acute coal shortages, currency expansion, and low urban food reserves hindered industrial recovery. In Korea, the Moscow Conference agreement proposing a four-power five-year trusteeship triggered nationwide strikes and mass protests led by Kim Koo, while General Hodge repudiated the authority of the Korean People's Republic. For historians, this report provides crucial statistical baselines from the November 1945 census, primary documentation of demilitarization policies, and essential evidence of early Cold War tensions across Northeast Asia.
